headline: Record-breaking King Tides plus a big incoming swell bring major, locally extreme coastal flooding to the Orange and San Diego County beaches Tuesday through Friday, while inland the week stays dry and turns warm, with Santa Ana winds and highs in the mid 70s to mid 80s west of the mountains on Thanksgiving and Friday.

sections.title: Today & Tonight
sections.text: A few showers fell overnight and early Monday morning, mostly over San Diego and Orange counties, with the most rain at North Island and Point Loma (0.14 inch) and 0.10 inch or less farther north and inland. The rest of Monday and Monday night are dry, with highs a few degrees warmer than Sunday, a few clouds over the foothills into early evening, and scattered high clouds drifting through overnight.

sections.title: Short Term
sections.text: Tuesday warms another 3–5 degrees under a passing area of high pressure and stays dry, with east winds gusting locally to about 35 mph Tuesday morning on the coast-facing foothill slopes. On Wednesday a low-pressure system aloft pushes that high pressure east, but it isn't expected to bring any significant weather: it stays dry, with just slight cooling west of the mountains, including the coast and valleys.

sections.title: Long Term
sections.text: Thanksgiving (Thursday) and Friday bring mainly weak, locally moderate Santa Ana winds (dry northeast winds blowing from inland toward the coast), with gusts of 35–45 mph in the mountains, foothills and passes; the strongest winds come Thursday, and 45 mph gusts should be limited to the usual windy spots. Both days are dry and warm, 5–15 degrees above average and warmest Friday, with highs from the mid to upper 70s to the mid 80s west of the mountains. Saturday cools a few degrees as low pressure approaches, and the forecast includes a chance of light rain Sunday, though only about 60 percent of computer model runs bring the storm close enough for rain, so confidence is low. A generally unsettled pattern may continue into the first week of December, with chances for more rain, cooler weather and westerly winds.

coast: Coastal flooding is the big hazard this week on the Orange County and San Diego County coasts. Morning high tides are climbing (7.73 feet at La Jolla on Monday morning) and will reach 7.9–8.3 feet Tuesday through Thursday, peaking Wednesday, about 1.1–1.2 feet above normal predictions, and will likely break the all-time tide records set in late October. Surf stays around 2–5 feet through Wednesday morning, then a large, long-period west swell (8–9 feet every 18–19 seconds) arrives late Wednesday into Thursday, bringing 6–8 foot breakers Thursday with sets of 10–12 feet on exposed west-facing beaches, lowering to 3–6 feet Friday. A Coastal Flood Advisory (moderate to locally major flooding at Tuesday morning's high tide) runs until 4 AM Tuesday, followed by a Coastal Flood Warning from 4 AM Tuesday to 1 PM Friday for major flooding, with locally extreme flooding expected during Thursday morning's high tide; a High Surf Advisory covers the San Diego County coast from 1 PM Wednesday to 4 AM Friday. For boaters, no hazards are expected through Tuesday; a Small Craft Advisory covers the outer waters (10–60 miles out, including San Clemente Island) from 10 AM Wednesday to 10 AM Thursday for combined seas of 8–12 feet and northwest winds of about 23–29 mph (20–25 knots) near San Clemente Island Wednesday afternoon and evening, with seas falling below 10 feet by Thursday evening.
watch_for: Major, locally extreme coastal flooding at the morning high tides Tuesday through Friday, worst Thursday when record tides meet 10–12 foot surf sets.
Santa Ana wind gusts of 35–45 mph in the mountains, foothills and passes on Thanksgiving and Friday, with warm, dry conditions.
Low-confidence chance of light rain Sunday and a possibly wetter, cooler start to December.
confidence: Forecasters are confident in dry weather through Saturday and in the record tides and coastal flooding, moderately confident in mostly weak Santa Ana winds Thursday and Friday (with slightly less uncertainty about where the low-pressure system ends up), and have low confidence in the details of rain chances Sunday into next week.
